analysis.title: Global Style Counselling: Multi-Factor strategies offer resilience and opportunity in a polarised market
key_insights: Cross-sectional dispersion has surged again in recent weeks and driven extreme factor performance. Momentum pulled back sharply, low-volatility stocks were the main beneficiaries, and value also outperformed. SG compares it to the summer momentum unwind.

US small caps are the exception. Most factors have performed well in recent weeks as speculative activity moderated. The speculative phase had favoured highly leveraged, volatile, unprofitable companies, the opposite of what most quant models target.

Momentum has given back virtually all of its YTD outperformance in the US and Japan after two pullbacks, one in the summer and one over the last month. European price momentum was less volatile and kept part of its gains.

Low versus high volatility mirrored the momentum reversal, with a strong recovery over recent weeks led by the US, Japan and Emerging Markets. Europe was more muted, and the factor is still well below its early 2025 peaks.

Much of the momentum reversal came from a sharp reversal in high-vol/beta stocks that had surged with the broader market. Residual (beta-adjusted) momentum and earnings momentum held up better, particularly in Japan. SG prefers residual momentum and favours a combined residual price plus earnings momentum signal.

US and Japan momentum remain tied to the AI trade: long US Semiconductors and Hardware, short Software. The main change is a meaningful reduction in the Software underweight. US momentum's Energy exposure has also risen significantly.

European price momentum is relatively insulated from AI, with no significant tech-related exposure and a large overweight in Banks. Japan keeps meaningful AI exposure and also has a significant Banks overweight.
The 12-month momentum definition excludes the latest month, so the past month's sharp moves will only affect momentum portfolios at next month's rebalance.

The recent momentum sell-off was driven by the long leg, unlike the summer unwind, which was driven by a rebound in the short leg. The short leg of low-vol, essentially the highest-volatility stocks, mirrored it. SG reads this as the latest rotation being more risk-off than the summer one.

The long and short legs of momentum and low-vol have moved in opposite directions. Both legs are long-only portfolios that would normally correlate highly. Their rolling 1-year correlation has fallen to levels last seen during COVID.

Average pairwise stock correlations are at historic lows and the share of negatively correlated pairs is at a record. In the S&P 500 about 35% of roughly 125,000 pairs, or about 44,000, are negatively correlated on a 1-year basis.

Energy is a top contributor to negatively correlated pairs in both the US and Europe. US Semiconductors, Hardware and Software are also large contributors. In Europe Banks are the key driver and tech plays a much smaller role. SG names three polarisation themes: oil volatility after the Middle East conflict, AI winners versus losers, and European bank performance.

Negative correlation dampens index volatility but amplifies long/short portfolio volatility when negatively correlated names sit on opposite sides of the book. This has produced several days of extreme daily returns this year in the US momentum and low-vol long/short portfolios.

SG's traditional and ML multi-factor long/short indices stayed resilient through the recent momentum rout and kept most of their gains from earlier in the year. Both hold meaningful momentum exposure and neither explicitly targets low volatility. They combine value, momentum and fundamental quality, and the ML version adds monthly and weekly ML signals.

The multi-factor strategies are beta-neutral and sector-neutral with ex-ante long/short volatility capped at 5%. They rebalance monthly, most recently at last Thursday's close, which reinforced beta neutrality and cut exposure to the most volatile stocks. The correlation between their long and short legs has stayed broadly unchanged through the year.

PCA of daily stock returns shows PC1, linked to the AI theme, explaining 27% of variance in Japan and 17% in the US, but it is subdued in Europe. PC2 appears to capture an energy and inflation dynamic that emerged with higher oil prices in Q1 2026. SG says sector classifications alone can understate AI and oil-sensitivity themes that cut across industries.

SG argues that high dispersion and low correlation raise the alpha opportunity set for systematic stock-picking. Its multi-factor strategies have historically delivered some of their strongest returns in low-correlation, high-dispersion regimes, based on annualised 1-month forward returns by correlation quintile.
risk_factors: Concentrated long/short factor exposures can be caught on the wrong side of the themes driving polarisation, such as AI and oil sensitivity, when return dispersion is high and correlations are low.
Negatively correlated stocks sitting on opposite sides of a long/short book amplify portfolio volatility, as seen in momentum and low-vol.
Momentum remains closely tied to the AI trade in the US and Japan, so it is exposed to moves in that theme once the past month's returns enter the signal at the next rebalance.
charts_described: Long/short momentum and low-vol leg correlation charts show the rolling 1-year correlation between legs falling to levels seen only during the COVID period.

Multi-factor annualised performance by correlation regime quintiles: the traditional index returns 10.0% in the lowest-correlation quintile versus -1.1% in the highest, and the ML version 10.3% versus 4.2%.
vol_and_positioning: Momentum has unwound twice (summer, then the last month), with the recent move led by the long leg and a risk-off tone. Low-vol outperformed as high-vol and high-beta stocks reversed.

US momentum remains long Semiconductors and Hardware and short Software, with a reduced Software underweight and higher Energy exposure. The 12m1m window means the recent sell-off only feeds into momentum portfolios at next month's rebalance.
The correlation between the long and short legs of momentum and low-vol has collapsed to COVID-era lows, which raises long/short portfolio volatility even as index-level volatility is suppressed.
Average pairwise correlation in the S&P 500 and Stoxx 600 is at historic lows, and the share of negatively correlated pairs is at a record. About 35% of S&P 500 pairs are negatively correlated.
geopolitical: Volatility in oil prices following the conflict in the Middle East is cited as one of three themes driving equity polarisation.

tension_points.bull_case: High dispersion and low correlations increase the opportunity set for alpha. Systematic stock-picking strategies are well positioned to exploit inefficiencies, and SG's multi-factor strategies have historically delivered some of their strongest performance in such regimes.
tension_points.bear_case: Negative correlations between longs and shorts amplify long/short portfolio volatility. Momentum and low-vol have seen the correlation between their legs collapse to COVID-era lows, with several extreme daily returns this year.

theme_stances.key_argument: Momentum has surrendered virtually all of its YTD outperformance in the US and Japan, and the latest drop was driven by the long leg.
theme_stances.evidence: Momentum strategies have suffered sharp unwinds

theme_stances.key_argument: Factor diversification and portfolio risk controls kept multi-factor performance smooth and most gains were retained, and high dispersion expands the alpha opportunity set.
Record negatively correlated stock pairs driven by oil volatility, AI winners versus losers and European banks are suppressing index volatility while amplifying long/short volatility.
